content: Typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever remain significant causes of morbidity and mortality, particularly in children and adolescents in South-Central and Southeast Asia. Two widely available vaccines for typhoid fever are the oral Ty21a vaccine and the injectable Vi polysaccharide vaccine. Newer typhoid conjugate vaccines, such as the Vi tetanus toxoid (Vi-TT) conjugate vaccine (Typbar-TCV), have been recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the preferred vaccine for all age groups. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of typhoid fever vaccines. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing typhoid vaccines with either other typhoid vaccines or placebo. Human challenge studies were excluded. Data were analyzed using the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence, and vaccine efficacy was calculated for up to three years of follow-up. Ty21a Vaccine (Oral, Three Doses) A three-dose regimen of the Ty21a vaccine likely prevents approximately 50% of typhoid fever cases over three years following vaccination (cumulative efficacy: 50%, 95% CI 35% to 61%; moderate-certainty evidence). This data is based on trials involving individuals aged 3 to 44 years. The vaccine does not appear to significantly increase the risk of vomiting, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, or rash compared to placebo (moderate-certainty evidence). However, fever is more commonly reported following vaccination (moderate-certainty evidence). Vi Polysaccharide Vaccine (Injectable, Single Dose) A single dose of the Vi polysaccharide vaccine prevents approximately 69% of typhoid cases in the first year after vaccination (95% CI 63% to 74%; high-certainty evidence). In the second year, efficacy decreases to approximately 59% (95% CI 45% to 69%; moderate-certainty evidence). Over three years, cumulative efficacy is estimated to be around 55% (95% CI 30% to 70%; low-certainty evidence). This data is derived from a single trial conducted in South Africa in the 1980s involving participants aged 5 to 15 years. The vaccine does not significantly increase the risk of fever or erythema compared to placebo (moderateand low-certainty evidence, respectively). However, swelling and pain at the injection site are more common in the vaccine group (moderate-certainty evidence). Vi-rEPA Vaccine (Injectable, Two Doses) Two doses of the Vi-rEPA vaccine likely prevent between 50% and 96% of typhoid cases during the first two years after vaccination (year 1: 94%, 95% CI 75% to 99%; year 2: 87%, 95% CI 56% to 96%; moderate-certainty evidence). This data is based on a single trial conducted in Vietnam involving children aged 2 to 5 years. Both the first and second doses of the vaccine increase the risk of fever (low-certainty evidence), and the second dose increases the incidence of swelling at the injection site (moderate-certainty evidence). Vi-TT Vaccine (Injectable, Two Doses) The efficacy of two doses of the Vi-TT vaccine (PedaTyph) in preventing typhoid fever in children during the first year after vaccination is uncertain (year 1: 94%, 95% CI −1% to 100%; very low-certainty evidence). This data is based on a single cluster-randomized trial conducted in India involving children aged 6 months to 12 years. For the single-dose Vi-TT vaccine (Typbar-TCV), no efficacy trials with natural exposure were identified. No serious adverse effects were reported in randomized controlled trials of any of the vaccines studied. Conclusions The licensed Ty21a and Vi polysaccharide vaccines are effective in preventing typhoid fever in adults and children older than two years in endemic regions. The Vi-rEPA vaccine also demonstrates efficacy, although data are limited to children. The newer Vi-TT vaccine (PedaTyph) requires further evaluation to confirm its protective effects against typhoid fever. Current data on the Vi-TT vaccine (Typbar-TCV) are limited to human challenge studies in adults, underscoring the need for ongoing field trials to assess its efficacy in real-world settings.
